name: Corrugated cardboard
curbside_basis: SPC 2020-21 Centralized Study on Availability of Recycling: corrugated boxes accepted for 88% of the U.S. population (87% explicit, 1% implicit; curbside and drop-off combined, not split).
carbon_boundary: cradle-to-gate, finished form where available; see carbon_reason

eol_split.basis: EPA 2018: 33.3M tons generated, ~32.1M recycled, 230k combusted, 940k landfilled (corrugated boxes).

disposal_text: Flatten the box and place it in your curbside recycling bin.
how2recycle_label: Widely Recyclable (inferred, not looked up in the How2Recycle Label Explorer: 88% access exceeds How2Recycle's 60% threshold)
contamination_notes: Keep it clean and dry; EPA says containers contaminated with food cannot be recycled. Flatten before recycling (EPA). Tape and shipping labels are normally fine, but this was not confirmed from a source opened for this research.
why_it_matters: Cardboard is the most-recycled packaging in the U.S., so a box that fits well is usually the lowest-waste way to protect a product.
notes: Recycle rate: EPA Facts and Figures, Containers and Packaging product-specific page (page updated Oct 19, 2026; data year 2018): 'The recycling rate for corrugated boxes was 96.5 percent.' CAUTION: AF&PA (industry, released Aug 28, 2026) reports 70%-75% of cardboard available for recovery was recycled in 2025 (https://www.afandpa.org/news/2026/paper-industry-announces-2025-us-paper-recycling-rates). The two use different methods; EPA's 2018 figure is used here so all materials share one data year and method. Carbon: WARM v16 Exhibit 3-11/3-12, corrugated containers RMAM 0.83 MTCO2E per short ton (process energy 0.67, transport 0.15, non-energy 0.01; WARM notes it includes at least 9.8% recycled content), converted at 0.907185 t per short ton. is_estimate is true because the carbon factor is always an estimate.
recycle_rate_reason: A box shipped to a home enters the residential stream. TRP's 32% is the end-to-end residential rate on the same method as every other material here. AF&PA's 70-75% and EPA's 96.5% are inflated for this use because they include retail and industrial back-of-store cardboard (and, for EPA 2018/old AF&PA, an undercounted denominator). EPA's 2019 residential estimate (53.5%) is a reasonable sensitivity case but uses state-reported per-capita data and does not cover film.

recycle_rate_options.publisher: The Recycling Partnership (State of Recycling 2024, Figure 14 'National Residential Recycling Rates by Material Category', Cardboard)
recycle_rate_options.notes: End-to-end residential rate. Published January 2024; National Database pulled Oct 20, 2023; participation inputs from 2020 survey, so data_year is approximate. Figure 18 national row matches. Resource Recycling (Jan 16, 2024, secondary) reports the same study as 'seven out of 10 cardboard boxes' going to the trash.

recycle_rate_options.notes: Residential sector only. Exhibit 2-1 gives tons (cardboard 34.2M generated, 18.3M recycled); rate is recycled/generated. Resource Recycling (Jan 28, 2025, secondary) reports the same 53.5%. Built from per-capita rates in Ball Corporation's 2021 '50 States of Recycling' report, not field measurement.

name: Kraft paper
curbside_basis: AF&PA: all-paper mailers 'can go in your curbside bin or be dropped off'. EPA common recyclables page covers paper generally. SPC 2020-21 access study did not study paper bags or kraft paper, so no access percentage is confirmed.
carbon_boundary: cradle-to-gate, finished form where available; see carbon_reason

eol_split.basis: EPA 2018 Table 5 subtotal 'Containers and Packaging excluding Corrugated Boxes' (bags and sacks, folding cartons, other paper packaging): 8,640k tons generated, 1,800k recycled, 1,340k combusted, 5,500k landfilled. No separate split for kraft paper.

disposal_text: Place clean, dry paper mailers and paper fill in your curbside recycling bin.
how2recycle_label: Unconfirmed (no Label Explorer lookup; SPC access study did not cover paper bags or kraft paper)
contamination_notes: Must be clean and dry; food-soiled paper cannot be recycled (EPA). Shiny or laminated coatings often make wrapping paper non-recyclable (EPA). Paper mailers with plastic bubble lining belong under paper-plastic-mix, not here.
why_it_matters: Paper fill and paper mailers can go in most recycling bins, but non-box paper packaging is recycled far less often than cardboard, so using less of it still matters.
notes: Recycle rate is a proxy: EPA paper and paperboard page gives a 20.8% 2018 recycling rate for 'paper containers and packaging, excluding corrugated boxes'; EPA 2018 Tables and Figures Table 5 confirms (8,640 generated, 1,800 recycled, thousand tons). EPA gives no separate rate for bags and sacks or wrapping paper. Tissue and crinkle paper may be treated differently by local programs; not confirmed. Carbon: WARM v16 Exhibit 3-11, office paper RMAM 0.97 MTCO2E per short ton (footnote 16: office paper is the proxy for bags and sacks, folding cartons and other paper packaging), converted to kg/kg.
recycle_rate_reason: No source measures kraft mailers, void fill or tissue directly. TRP mixed paper (23%) is the closest residential category and uses the same method as film. EPA's 20.8% proxy is not a measurement of kraft mailers (it is mostly folding cartons, all sectors), but it lands close to TRP's residential mixed-paper rate, so it was not the main distortion. The bigger distortion in the demo was pe-film's 10%, an all-sector EPA number, versus TRP's residential film rate of under 1%. Tissue and crinkle paper may be rejected by some programs; not confirmed.

recycle_rate_options.publisher: The Recycling Partnership (State of Recycling 2024, Figure 14, Mixed Paper)
recycle_rate_options.notes: Proxy: TRP has no kraft-paper or mailer category. Mixed paper is the conservative mapping.

recycle_rate_options.publisher: The Recycling Partnership (State of Recycling 2024, Figure 14, Cardboard)
recycle_rate_options.notes: Alternative proxy if kraft mailers are treated as entering the cardboard stream. AF&PA survey says paper padded mailers are accepted by members representing 85% of mixed paper consumption and 83% of OCC consumption, so mills take them in both streams.
